subject: question about the transformed parameter block

messages.author: bfef42e54ffcc8b5
messages.subject: question about the transformed parameter block
parts:
fellow stan users,

i am a stan rookie and a stan fan.

my question is about what to put in the "model" block and what to put
in the "transformed parameters" block. specifically, why and when do
transformed parameters speed up sampling? my tenuous understanding is
that the parameters are transformed just as often as the model block
is computed about. is that incorrect?

FYI, i am using stan to implement variants of matt taddy's inverse
regression for text. the original model can be found here:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2098

it's a multinomial regression with a high-dimensional (6000) & sparse
response and few covariates (1-3).

best
dave

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] question about the transformed parameter block
parts:
Hi Dave,

There's no computational difference (that I know of) between doing the
transformations in the model or transformed parameter block. The main
difference is that if something's in transformed parameters then it'll
get saved—it's just a convenience thing.

Best,
Matt

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] question about the transformed parameter block
parts:
On Tuesday, March 5, 2013 11:16:32 AM UTC-5, Matt Hoffman wrote:
There's no computational difference (that I know of) between doing the
transformations in the model or transformed parameter block. The main
difference is that if something's in transformed parameters then it'll
get saved—it's just a convenience thing.

Minor addition: In the transformed parameters block, any stated restrictions on the support of the transformed parameter are checked every time the log-posterior is evaluated, but there are no such checks in the model block (and I think trying to restrict the support of a local variable in the model block will result in a compiler error). So

parameters {
  real<lower=0> sd;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> variance;
  variance = sd * sd; // Stan will verify that variance is non-negative with some minor cost
}
model {
  real precision;
  precision = 1 / variance; // Stan does not verify that precision is non-negative
}

This really only makes a difference if the checking is non-trivial, such as with large covariance matrices and whatnot.

Ben


Ben

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] question about the transformed parameter block
parts:
Hi Dave,

The additional benefit of using the transformed parameter block is the ability to use constraints on the variables. The constraints are checked once per leapfrog step, which adds a little computational overhead, but can help trap modeling errors early.

If you want a more detailed explanation, there is a chapter in the manual on Program Blocks. The overview subsection discusses how frequently each of the blocks are executed.


Daniel
